description: Paid padding share on a SMALLER model, testing the direction review M2 identifies as the first-order threat. Quantization halves the per-chip weight floor; so does a smaller model, and we already have one qualified. The TP ablation established that a LARGER floor makes padding cheaper, so a smaller floor must make it more expensive.
note_seq_len: Per-sequence length is near-constant within an edge (128 vs 130) on purpose. Comparing 4x96 against 4x128 would move sequence length by a third, changing attention work materially and destroying the clean prediction that cost is proportional to real tokens.
note_single_step: Both edges sit far below max_num_batched_tokens=8192 so the scheduler has no reason to split. Every dispatch records its step count and splits are counted, not averaged over: a split reintroduces exactly the smearing this experiment exists to avoid.
note_prediction: REGISTERED BEFORE MEASUREMENT. TinyLlama-1.1B at TP=4 puts ~0.55 GB of bf16 weights per chip against Qwen3-4B's 2.01 GB — a 3.6x smaller floor. If the mechanism is the weight floor, the paid share at n=4 and n=8 must be HIGHER than Qwen3-4B's 23.1% and 14.3%. If it is unchanged, the mechanism is not the floor and §4.5 is wrong.
note_limits: max_model_len is 2048 because TinyLlama's max_position_embeddings is; check_model.py caught this before the boot rather than after. max_num_batched_tokens stays above it so an n=8 dispatch of ~2064 tokens is not split by the token limit, which would reintroduce exactly the smearing this experiment excludes.
prediction_mechanism: INVALID, and recorded as such. Target: arithmetic intensity = FLOPs/bytes. Lever: parameter count P. But bytes = 2P and FLOPs/token = 2P, so intensity = 1 independent of P and the derivative is ZERO. This lever cannot move the target; quantization can, because it halves bytes and leaves FLOPs alone.
